note: Bibliography for rubric.md and dimensions.json. URLs were checked to resolve on 2026-10-21; ISO, IEEE and INCOSE pages may require a browser or purchase. 'kind' groups sources as in the survey section of rubric.md.

references.title: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering
references.used_for: Characteristics of individual requirements (necessary, appropriate, unambiguous, complete, singular, feasible, verifiable, correct, conforming) and of requirement sets (complete, consistent, feasible, comprehensible, able to be validated); implementation-free statement of need.

references.title: INCOSE Guide to Writing Requirements (GtWR), version 4
references.used_for: Characteristics C1–C15 and writing rules, including solution-free statements, avoidance of vague and escape-clause terms, consistent terminology and traceability.

references.title: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 Software, systems and enterprise — Architecture description
references.used_for: Architecture descriptions identify stakeholders and their concerns and record decisions with their rationale and the alternatives considered.

references.title: ISO 24495-1:2023 Plain language — Part 1: Governing principles and guidelines
references.used_for: Four governing principles: readers get what they need (relevant), can easily find it (findable), can easily understand it (understandable) and can use it (usable).

references.title: Federal Plain Language Guidelines (PLAIN, plainlanguage.gov)
references.used_for: Write for the audience, organize to meet readers' needs, omit excess words, use defined terms consistently, put the main point first.

references.title: Google developer documentation style guide
references.used_for: Conversational but precise technical prose, consistent terminology, putting conditions before instructions, avoiding filler.

references.title: Microsoft Writing Style Guide
references.used_for: Get to the point fast; short, scannable sentences; consistent terms.

references.title: GOV.UK content design: writing for GOV.UK
references.used_for: Front-load the important information; write for user need rather than organizational structure.

references.title: Write the Docs: Documentation principles
references.used_for: ARID (accept some repetition in documentation), skimmable, exemplary, consistent, complete; repetition that serves the reader is not automatically waste.

references.title: Diátaxis: a systematic approach to technical documentation authoring (D. Procida)
references.used_for: Documents serve distinct needs; mixing purposes (explanation inside reference, implementation steps inside a decision record) degrades each.

references.title: AAC&U VALUE Rubric: Written Communication
references.used_for: Published analytic rubric with criteria: context of and purpose for writing; content development; genre and disciplinary conventions; sources and evidence; control of syntax and mechanics.

references.title: 6+1 Trait Writing model (Education Northwest)
references.used_for: Analytic traits: ideas, organization, voice, word choice, sentence fluency, conventions, presentation; the canonical example of scoring traits separately rather than holistically.

references.title: PEP 1 — PEP Purpose and Guidelines
references.used_for: What belongs in a successful PEP: abstract, motivation, rationale, specification, backwards compatibility, security implications, how to teach this, reference implementation, rejected ideas, open issues.

references.title: PEP 12 — Sample reStructuredText PEP Template
references.used_for: Required header fields and section order for PEPs.

references.title: Rust RFC template (rust-lang/rfcs 0000-template.md)
references.used_for: Summary, motivation, guide-level then reference-level explanation (explicit overview-before-detail progression), drawbacks, rationale and alternatives, prior art, unresolved questions, future possibilities.

references.title: Kubernetes KEP template (kubernetes/enhancements NNNN-kep-template)
references.used_for: Summary, motivation, goals and non-goals, proposal, risks and mitigations, design details, test plan, graduation criteria, alternatives.

references.title: Go proposal process (golang/proposal README)
references.used_for: Design documents follow discussion of a short proposal; the design doc states background, proposal, rationale, compatibility, implementation and open issues.

references.title: RFC 7322 — RFC Style Guide
references.used_for: Required RFC sections, consistent terminology and abbreviation expansion, clarity and consistency as editorial goals.

references.title: RFC 8174 — Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words
references.used_for: Requirement-level keywords (MUST, SHOULD, MAY) make obligation explicit and unambiguous.

references.title: RFC 4101 — Writing Protocol Models (E. Rescorla)
references.used_for: Detail written for implementors gets in the way of initial understanding; give reviewers a model in overview form first.

references.title: RFC 3552 — Guidelines for Writing RFC Text on Security Considerations
references.used_for: Documents must state threats, what is and is not in scope, and residual risk explicitly.

references.title: Oxide RFD 1 — Requests for Discussion
references.used_for: RFDs record ideas at early states (prediscussion, ideation, discussion) and are expected to state the problem and open questions honestly rather than present settled detail.

references.title: Shape Up, Chapter 6: Write the Pitch (R. Singer, Basecamp)
references.used_for: Five pitch ingredients: problem, appetite, solution, rabbit holes, no-gos.

references.title: Shape Up, Principles of Shaping (R. Singer, Basecamp)
references.used_for: Shaped work is rough, solved and bounded; wireframes are too concrete and words are too abstract — the right level of detail.

references.title: Design Docs at Google (M. Ubl, industrialempathy.com)
references.used_for: Context and scope, goals and non-goals, design, alternatives considered, cross-cutting concerns; design docs that are really implementation manuals add little.

references.title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook (NASA/SP-2016-6105 Rev 2)
references.used_for: Appendix C: how to write a good requirement (verifiable, traceable, implementation-free); concept studies state assumptions and trade studies.

references.title: Gopen, G. D. and Swan, J. A. The Science of Scientific Writing. American Scientist 78(6):550–558
references.used_for: Reader expectations: old information before new, topic position links backward, stress position carries the new point; progression failures make readers reconstruct the logic.

references.title: Minto, B. The Pyramid Principle: Logic in Writing and Thinking (3rd ed.). Pearson
references.used_for: Start with the governing idea, then group and order supporting points so each level summarizes the one below.

references.title: Grice, H. P. Logic and Conversation. In Cole and Morgan (eds.), Syntax and Semantics 3: Speech Acts, 41–58
references.used_for: Maxims of quantity (as informative as required, no more), quality (do not say what lacks evidence), relation (be relevant) and manner (be perspicuous, orderly).

references.title: Williams, J. M. and Bizup, J. Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace (12th ed.). Pearson
references.used_for: Concision by deleting meaningless, redundant and implied words; coherence through consistent topic strings.

references.title: Gotel, O. and Finkelstein, A. An Analysis of the Requirements Traceability Problem. Proc. IEEE ICRE, 94–101
references.used_for: Pre-requirements traceability: being able to follow a requirement back to the statements and people it came from.

references.title: Graesser, A. C., McNamara, D. S., Louwerse, M. M. and Cai, Z. Coh-Metrix: Analysis of text on cohesion and language. Behavior Research Methods 36:193–202
references.used_for: Automatic cohesion indices (referential overlap, connectives, latent semantic overlap between adjacent sections).

references.title: Halliday, M. A. K. and Hasan, R. Cohesion in English. Longman
references.used_for: Reference, substitution, ellipsis, conjunction and lexical cohesion tie a passage to the text before it.

references.title: Fabbri, A. R. et al. SummEval: Re-evaluating Summarization Evaluation. TACL 9
references.used_for: Separately annotated dimensions (coherence, consistency, fluency, relevance) and weak correlation of surface metrics with them.

references.title: Liu, Y. et al. G-Eval: NLG Evaluation using GPT-4 with Better Human Alignment
references.used_for: Per-dimension LLM judging with explicit criteria and evaluation steps; judges prefer LLM-written text.

references.title: Kim, S. et al. Prometheus: Inducing Fine-grained Evaluation Capability in Language Models
references.used_for: Rubric-conditioned judging with score anchors per level and feedback before score.

references.title: Min, S. et al. FActScore: Fine-grained Atomic Evaluation of Factual Precision in Long Form Text Generation
references.used_for: Decompose text into atomic claims and check each against a knowledge source.

references.title: Laban, P. et al. SummaC: Re-Visiting NLI-based Models for Inconsistency Detection in Summarization. TACL 10
references.used_for: Sentence-level entailment between source and output as an inconsistency detector.

references.title: Kryściński, W. et al. Evaluating the Factual Consistency of Abstractive Text Summarization. EMNLP
references.used_for: Model-based consistency checking against the source document.

references.title: Wang, A., Cho, K. and Lewis, M. Asking and Answering Questions to Evaluate the Factual Consistency of Summaries. ACL
references.used_for: Question generation from the output and answering against the source; adaptable to requirement coverage (questions from the brief answered against the draft).

references.title: Zheng, L. et al. Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena. NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks
references.used_for: Position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases of LLM judges; swap-order evaluation.

references.title: Saito, K. et al. Verbosity Bias in Preference Labeling by Large Language Models
references.used_for: LLM judges prefer longer answers beyond human preference.

references.title: Dubois, Y. et al. Length-Controlled AlpacaEval: A Simple Way to Debias Automatic Evaluators
references.used_for: Regression-based length control for automatic preference judges.

references.title: Huang, H. et al. An Empirical Study of LLM-as-a-Judge for LLM Evaluation: Fine-tuned Judge Model is not a General Substitute for GPT-4
references.used_for: Rubric-specialised judges generalize poorly across aspects; calibration per dimension is required.

references.title: Burrows, J. 'Delta': a Measure of Stylistic Difference and a Guide to Likely Authorship. Literary and Linguistic Computing 17(3):267–287
references.used_for: Function-word frequency distance as a stylometric signal; used here only to detect style-match bias, not as quality.

references.title: Vale: a syntax-aware prose linter
references.used_for: Rule-based detection of filler phrases, weasel words, inconsistent terms; a source of automatic candidate measures.
